qs.q: What is the main focus of the Data Structures topic in this course?

c.x: Organizing and storing data for efficient access
Writing correct syntax in a programming language
Designing the physical layout of computer hardware
Managing user permissions across a network

qs.e: Data structures are techniques for organizing and storing data so that it can be accessed and modified efficiently.

qs.q: What is the main focus of the Algorithms topic in this course?

c.x: Step-by-step procedures to solve problems or manipulate data
Physical storage layouts of files on a hard disk
Rules for formatting text inside a document
Methods for connecting devices over a network

qs.e: Algorithms are step-by-step procedures used to solve problems or manipulate data.

qs.q: Which of the following notations is used for asymptotic analysis of an algorithm's time and space complexity?

c.x: Big-O notation
HTML tag syntax
SQL query syntax
Regular expression syntax

qs.e: Big-O, along with Omega and Theta, is used for asymptotic analysis to measure time and space complexity.

qs.q: Which ordering principle does a queue data structure follow?

c.x: First-in, first-out
Last-in, first-out
Random access order
Priority-based order

qs.e: A queue follows the first-in, first-out (FIFO) principle, in contrast to a stack's last-in, first-out (LIFO) principle.

qs.q: What principle governs how elements are inserted and removed in a stack?

c.x: Last-in, first-out
First-in, first-out
Smallest value first
Random selection order

qs.e: A stack is a collection of objects inserted and removed according to the last-in, first-out (LIFO) principle.

qs.q: Which element can a user directly access or remove from a stack at any given time?

c.x: Only the most recently inserted element
Any element at any position in the stack
Only the very first element ever inserted
Only elements stored at even positions

qs.e: A user may only access or remove the most recently inserted object, which is the top of the stack.

qs.q: What does it mean to describe stacks and queues as 'restricted access' structures?

c.x: Only one item can be read or removed at a time
Any number of items can be changed at once
Items must always be stored in sorted order
Items are limited to a single fixed data type

qs.e: In a stack or queue, access is restricted: only one item can be read or removed at a time.

qs.q: Why are stacks and queues considered more abstract than arrays?

c.x: They are defined primarily by their interface
They can only be built using linked lists
They can never be implemented using an array
They must always store a fixed number of items

qs.e: Stacks and queues are defined primarily by their interface; their underlying mechanism can be an array, a linked list, or something else.

qs.q: What does the push(e) operation do on a stack S?

c.x: Adds element e to the top of stack S
Removes the top element of stack S
Returns the top element of stack S
Returns the size of stack S

qs.e: S.push(e) adds element e to the top of stack S.

qs.q: What does the pop() operation do on a stack S?

c.x: Adds a new element to the top of stack S
Removes and returns the top element of S
Returns the top element without removing it
Checks whether stack S is currently empty

qs.e: S.pop() removes and returns the top element from stack S.

qs.q: What does the top() operation do on a stack S?

c.x: Removes and returns the top element of S
Adds a new element to the top of stack S
Returns the top element without removing it
Returns the number of elements in S

qs.e: S.top() returns a reference to the top element of stack S, without removing it.

qs.q: What does S.is_empty() return for a stack S?

c.x: True if stack S contains no elements at all
The total number of elements in stack S
The top element currently stored in S
True if stack S has at least one element

qs.e: S.is_empty() returns True if stack S does not contain any elements.

qs.q: Starting from an empty stack S, after calling S.push(5) followed by S.push(3), what does len(S) return?
qs.e: After pushing 5 and then 3, the stack holds two elements, so len(S) returns 2.

qs.q: Starting from an empty stack S, calls are made in this order: S.push(5), S.push(3), S.pop(). What value is returned by the S.pop() call?

c.x: error

qs.e: Since 3 was pushed last, it is on top of the stack, so S.pop() removes and returns 3.

qs.q: Starting from an empty stack S, calls are made in this order: S.push(7), S.push(9). What value does S.top() return?

c.x: error

qs.e: Since 9 was pushed last, it sits on top of the stack, so S.top() returns 9 without removing it.

qs.q: What happens when S.pop() is called on a stack S that currently has no elements?

c.x: An error occurs, since there is nothing to remove
It returns zero as a default empty value
It first pushes a default element automatically
It silently does nothing and returns nothing

qs.e: Calling pop() on an empty stack results in an error, since there is no top element to remove.

qs.q: In the simple array-based stack implementation, where is the top of the stack stored within the underlying Python list?

c.x: In the rightmost cell of the list
In the leftmost cell of the list
In the middle cell of the list
In a cell separate from the list

qs.e: The stack is implemented with a Python list, storing the top element in the rightmost cell of the list.

qs.q: What is the main idea behind the adapter design pattern used for this stack implementation?

c.x: Wrap an existing class and implement methods using it
Rewrite the Python list class entirely from scratch
Store every stack element in a separate database
Replace all list methods with new global functions

qs.e: The adapter pattern defines a new class containing an instance of the existing class as a hidden field, implementing each method using that hidden instance.

qs.q: Using the Python list adapter, which list operation realizes the stack's push(e) method?

c.x: L.append(e)
L.insert(0, e)
len(L)

qs.e: S.push(e) is realized as L.append(e), adding the new item to the end of the list.

qs.q: Using the Python list adapter, which expression realizes the stack's top() method?

c.x: L.append(e)
L.pop(0)
len(L)

qs.e: S.top() is realized as L[-1], returning the last item of the list without removing it.

qs.q: Using the Python list adapter, which expression realizes the stack's is_empty() method?

c.x: len(L) == 0
L.append(e) == 0
len(L) == 1

qs.e: S.is_empty() is realized as len(L) == 0, checking whether the underlying list has zero elements.

qs.q: What is the running time of the push and pop operations in the array-based stack implementation?

c.x: Amortized O(1)
Guaranteed worst-case O(1)
O(n) in every single case
O(log n) on average

qs.e: The O(1) time for push and pop are amortized bounds, not guaranteed on every single call.

qs.q: What is the running time of the top(), is_empty(), and len() operations in the array-based stack implementation?

c.x: Worst-case O(1)
Amortized O(1) only
O(n) in the worst case
O(n log n) on average

qs.e: The implementations for top, is_empty, and len use constant time in the worst case.

qs.q: Which of the following is described as a typical real-world use case for a stack?

c.x: Undo functionality in a text editor
Sorting a list of numbers by value
Storing records in alphabetical order
Scheduling packets by network priority

qs.e: Undo functionality in text editors is a listed use case, where actions are stored in a stack and undo means popping the latest action.

qs.q: In an undo feature implemented with a stack, how is the most recent action undone?

c.x: By popping the latest action off the stack
By pushing a brand new action onto the stack
By checking whether the stack is empty
By reading the bottom element of the stack

qs.e: Undo is implemented by popping the latest action from the stack that stores the sequence of actions.

qs.q: In the reverse_file function, why does writing the popped lines back to the file produce a reversed order?

c.x: Because a stack removes elements in last-in, first-out order
Because the file is read twice from start to end
Because Python lists are automatically kept sorted
Because lines are resorted alphabetically before writing

qs.e: Each line is pushed while reading, then popped while writing, and since a stack pops in last-in, first-out order, the lines come out reversed.

qs.q: While scanning an expression in the matching parentheses example, what gets pushed onto the stack?

c.x: Each opening delimiter encountered
Each closing delimiter encountered
Every single character in the expression
Only delimiters that fail to match

qs.e: Each opening symbol is pushed onto the stack, while each closing symbol is popped and checked against it.

qs.q: In the is_matched function, what happens if a closing delimiter is found while the stack is empty?

c.x: The function returns False immediately
The function returns True immediately
The closing delimiter is pushed instead
The scan restarts from the first character

qs.e: If the stack is empty when a closing delimiter appears, there is nothing to match it with, so the function returns False.

qs.q: Why is the expression 'a[b{c}d]e}' considered an incorrect delimiter match?

c.x: The final } has no matching opening delimiter
The ] symbol appears before any [ symbol
The letter c is repeated inside the brackets
There are too many letters between the delimiters

qs.e: All delimiters up to 'e' match correctly, but the final } has nothing left on the stack to pair with, since the stack is already empty.

qs.q: Why is the expression 'a{b(c)l' considered an incorrect delimiter match?

c.x: The opening { is never matched by a closing symbol
The ( symbol is closed before it is ever opened
There are two opening delimiters in a row
The letter l is an invalid character to use

qs.e: The ( and ) pair matches correctly, but the opening { pushed at the start is left on the stack with nothing to close it.
